articles.title: Redesigning International Order for a G-Minus World
articles.full_text:
This is the age of hyper-multipolarity, where every plausible steering group is missing something essential.
Leaders pose for a photo at the 52nd G7 summit in Evian, France, June 16, 2026.
Debates about international order usually begin with the same question: who will lead next? Will the United States recover its authority? Will China mature into a responsible provider of public goods? Will some concert of major powers manage the transition?
The question is familiar and increasingly misleading. The defining condition of this century is not a clean transfer of hegemony from one state to another. It is the erosion of the possibility that any single state, or compact group of great powers, can supply order for everyone else.
We live in a G-minus world. The term does not simply mean that leadership is absent, as in a G-zero world. It means that every plausible steering group is missing something essential. Military reach, manufacturing capacity, financial credibility, technological innovation, demographic weight, regulatory authority, and political legitimacy are distributed across different actors. The United States remains pre-eminent in several domains, but it depends on production networks it does not control. China is central to global manufacturing and trade, but lacks the alliance structure and financial trust to underwrite a universal order. The European Union can set standards, but cannot by itself secure the system it regulates. India, Brazil, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and other consequential powers cannot be treated as rule-takers, yet they do not form a coherent governing coalition.
This is more than multipolarity. It is hyper-multipolarity: power fragmented not only among states, but across domains. Strength in one arena no longer converts automatically into authority in another.
The older theory of hegemonic stability assumed that a dominant state would supply public goods because it possessed both the capacity and the incentive to do so. Today, those two dimensions have separated. The cost of underwriting open markets, dispute settlement, maritime security, financial stability, and crisis response has risen, while the domestic political return has become less certain. Great powers are therefore tempted not only to withdraw from order, but to extract from it, through tariffs, sanctions, coercive finance, and the weaponization of interdependence.
The response cannot be to ask middle powers to become a substitute hegemon. They lack the resources, and a coalition assigned hegemonic burdens would reproduce the same incentive problem on a smaller base. The more promising question is different: how can institutions make cooperation the rational choice even when no actor can command the system?
Recent experience provides three useful answers.
First, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership survived the United States’ withdrawal from its predecessor. The remaining members preserved high-standard rules, brought the agreement into force, and later admitted the United Kingdom. The result is not a replacement for the global trading system. It is something more practical: a functioning arrangement that creates benefits for members and opportunity costs for outsiders.
Second, when the World Trade Organization (WTO) Appellate Body became unable to hear appeals, a group of WTO members initiated the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement. More than 60 WTO members now participate, and the mechanism has produced actual arbitration outcomes. It is an imperfect bridge, but it demonstrates that institutional function need not wait for unanimity.
Third, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) binds 15 politically diverse economies representing roughly 30 percent of global output and population. RCEP is less ambitious than the CPTPP in several areas, but that is partly the point. ASEAN’s central role and the agreement’s differentiated obligations made cooperation possible among states that would not accept a single power’s blueprint.
These cases suggest three design principles for a G-minus world.
The first is modularity. The next order will not be one grand covenant. It will be a set of independent but connectable modules: digital trade, critical minerals, carbon accounting, AI governance, dispute settlement, supply chain resilience, financial transparency, maritime safety, and public health. Each module must be useful on its own and more valuable when linked to others.
The second is differentiated participation. Institutions should abandon the fiction that every participant must assume identical obligations at the same speed. A state may be a core member in digital trade, a partial participant in supply chain cooperation, and an observer in security discussions. Graduated participation is not institutional weakness. It is how diverse states enter cooperation without surrendering all autonomy at once.
The third is visible benefit. Cooperation fails when costs are immediate and gains are abstract. Good institutional design front-loads practical value: faster customs treatment, mutual certification, shared stockpiles, access to trusted markets, lower financing costs, usable dispute resolution, and credible insurance against disruption. The institution becomes durable when governments can show that participation pays.
This also clarifies what democratic multilateralism should mean. Democracies do not have a monopoly on benefits to participation, and non-democracies offer genuine incentives to engagement: infrastructure finance, energy, market access, security assistance, and diplomatic protection. An incentive is not a bribe; it is what economists model as self-interest. The difference should lie in structure. Patron-client incentives are discretionary and asymmetric. An incentive-based democratic institution should be rules-based, reciprocal, transparent, contestable, and open to additional participants that willingly agree to abide by those rules.
The goal is not to restore liberal internationalism at its imagined peak. That order was never as universal or benign as its defenders remember. A more realistic objective is a multilateral-enough world: enough rules that disputes do not default to coercion; enough openness that smaller economies can reach scale; enough redundancy that one institution’s paralysis does not become system-wide failure; and enough predictability that governments and firms can plan.
Waiting for Washington to return to a leadership role and waiting for Beijing to become responsible are mirror versions of the same mistake: both entrust order to power. In a G-minus world, great power companionship and permission are optional. Small states and middle powers cannot replace hegemony, but they can build around its absence. The task is to stop asking who will rule the international system and instead start designing a system that states will choose to remain in.
This essay is one of four to emerge from discussions at an international conference jointly organized by the Seoul Forum for International Affairs and the Hairan Series of Korea University’s Institute for Interdisciplinary Unification Studies, “Democratic Multilateralism at the Edge,” held in Seoul on April 20, 2026. 
Debates about international order usually begin with the same question: who will lead next? Will the United States recover its authority? Will China mature into a responsible provider of public goods? Will some concert of major powers manage the transition?
The question is familiar and increasingly misleading. The defining condition of this century is not a clean transfer of hegemony from one state to another. It is the erosion of the possibility that any single state, or compact group of great powers, can supply order for everyone else.
We live in a G-minus world. The term does not simply mean that leadership is absent, as in a G-zero world. It means that every plausible steering group is missing something essential. Military reach, manufacturing capacity, financial credibility, technological innovation, demographic weight, regulatory authority, and political legitimacy are distributed across different actors. The United States remains pre-eminent in several domains, but it depends on production networks it does not control. China is central to global manufacturing and trade, but lacks the alliance structure and financial trust to underwrite a universal order. The European Union can set standards, but cannot by itself secure the system it regulates. India, Brazil, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and other consequential powers cannot be treated as rule-takers, yet they do not form a coherent governing coalition.
This is more than multipolarity. It is hyper-multipolarity: power fragmented not only among states, but across domains. Strength in one arena no longer converts automatically into authority in another.
The older theory of hegemonic stability assumed that a dominant state would supply public goods because it possessed both the capacity and the incentive to do so. Today, those two dimensions have separated. The cost of underwriting open markets, dispute settlement, maritime security, financial stability, and crisis response has risen, while the domestic political return has become less certain. Great powers are therefore tempted not only to withdraw from order, but to extract from it, through tariffs, sanctions, coercive finance, and the weaponization of interdependence.
The response cannot be to ask middle powers to become a substitute hegemon. They lack the resources, and a coalition assigned hegemonic burdens would reproduce the same incentive problem on a smaller base. The more promising question is different: how can institutions make cooperation the rational choice even when no actor can command the system?
Recent experience provides three useful answers.
First, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership survived the United States’ withdrawal from its predecessor. The remaining members preserved high-standard rules, brought the agreement into force, and later admitted the United Kingdom. The result is not a replacement for the global trading system. It is something more practical: a functioning arrangement that creates benefits for members and opportunity costs for outsiders.
Second, when the World Trade Organization (WTO) Appellate Body became unable to hear appeals, a group of WTO members initiated the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement. More than 60 WTO members now participate, and the mechanism has produced actual arbitration outcomes. It is an imperfect bridge, but it demonstrates that institutional function need not wait for unanimity.
Third, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) binds 15 politically diverse economies representing roughly 30 percent of global output and population. RCEP is less ambitious than the CPTPP in several areas, but that is partly the point. ASEAN’s central role and the agreement’s differentiated obligations made cooperation possible among states that would not accept a single power’s blueprint.
articles.summary: This is the age of hyper-multipolarity, where every plausible steering group is missing something essential.

articles.title: Why the Bangsamoro Peace Process Still Depends on Trust
articles.full_text:
Elections set for September 14 will mark an important step forward, but the peace process will continue for long after the ballots have been counted.
The flag of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)’s first parliamentary elections, scheduled for September 14 after years of postponement, will complete one of the central political commitments under the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB): the transition from an appointed government to an elected one.
This milestone, however, will not mark the end of the peace process writ large.
The appointment in mid-July of a new chair of the Philippine Government Peace Implementing Panel illustrates why the implementation of the CAB remains an ongoing political process. After months without a permanent government counterpart to the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), a vacancy that had prompted the MILF to temporarily pause some peace process engagements, the appointment restored the principal bilateral mechanism responsible for implementing the CAB. More importantly, it signals that the difficult work of implementing the agreement will continue long after the ballots are counted.
Earlier this year, I argued that the elections would test the Bangsamoro peace process. That remains true, but just as important is the question of what comes after them. The remaining commitments under the CAB, including the completion of the decommissioning of combatants, the socioeconomic transformation of war camps, the dismantling of private armed groups, and transitional justice, still require sustained cooperation between the Philippine government and the MILF regardless of who wins the elections.
This challenge has become increasingly visible over recent months.
The MILF, long accustomed to operating as a relatively unified movement, has entered a period of genuine electoral competition. The United Bangsamoro Justice Party, led by many of the movement’s senior political leaders and peace negotiators, now competes against the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, which draws support from several former MILF commanders alongside established regional politicians. The Commission on Elections (COMELEC)’s recognition of the two parties as the region’s dominant majority and dominant minority political parties institutionalized the electoral competition that had emerged within the MILF itself.
None of these developments represents a failure of political normalization. Peace agreements are expected to transform armed opposition into democratic competition, and political differences are inevitable. The question is whether those differences continue to be managed through democratic institutions rather than through force of arms.
This question has become more pressing as the elections approach.
COMELEC has placed several areas in the BARMM under its highest category of election concern because of longstanding security risks.  Recent localized attacks on military detachments have also prompted the Philippine government and the MILF, through the Coordinating Committee on the Cessation of Hostilities (CCCH), to jointly condemn the violence, warning that it threatens not only public safety but also the gains of the peace process.
The MILF’s decision to temporarily pause its bilateral peace process engagements with the national government did not extend to the ceasefire architecture established under the CAB.  The continued operation of peace implementing mechanisms such as the CCCH and the Ad Hoc Joint Action Group, therefore, demonstrates the MILF’s decision to preserve security cooperation with the Armed Forces of the Philippines despite growing strains in its political relationship with the national government.
Political tensions have also become more visible within Bangsamoro communities. Legal petitions on the constitutionality of the leadership and composition of the interim Bangsamoro government, parliamentary scrutiny of governance, and successive public rallies in Cotabato City framed respectively around anti-corruption and accountability and the faithful implementation of the CAB reflected concerns, both in BARMM and national arenas, about the political legitimacy of the transition.
As divisions within the MILF became more pronounced, governance and implementation of the peace agreement increasingly came to be associated with two factions of the movement: the interim Bangsamoro government, which exercised regional executive authority during the transition, and the MILF leadership, which remained the principal signatory to the peace agreement.
This emerging political divide also reshaped the narrative surrounding the  Bangsamoro transition. For some local observers, the political messaging of both the national government and the interim Bangsamoro leadership increasingly framed the transition in terms of governance reforms and the forthcoming parliamentary elections rather than the continuing implementation of the CAB. While governance and elections are indispensable, such emphasis also risked reinforcing the view that the success of the Bangsamoro project would be measured primarily by governmental performance rather than by completion of the CAB that made the BARMM possible.
It was in this political environment that perceptions of national government involvement in the BARMM assumed greater significance. The issue was not Manila’s continued engagement in regional government’s affairs, which is inherent in the asymmetrical relationship between the national government and the BARMM established under the CAB, but whether that engagement was perceived to privilege governance and the electoral process over the continuing implementation of the peace agreement.
Such a distinction obscures the nature of the Bangsamoro transition. BARMM did not emerge independently of the peace process; it is one of its principal outcomes. Good governance and faithful implementation of the CAB should reinforce one another rather than being treated as competing priorities. The challenge now is to sustain the confidence necessary for the Philippine government and the MILF to carry the peace process through and beyond the elections.
This is why the appointment of a new Government Peace Implementing Panel chair is an important development.
Beyond filling a vacant position, the appointment restores a political counterpart for engagement with the MILF at a time when implementation has become more complex and confidence between the parties has come under greater strain. Mel Senen Sarmiento, who was appointed Secretary of the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation, and Unity (OPAPRU) in April, following leadership changes in the government’s peace office amid public criticism of his predecessor, now also chairs the Government Peace Implementing Panel for the Bangsamoro peace process.  By vesting both responsibilities in a Cabinet Member, the Philippine government has linked responsibility for overseeing peace policy with its principal mechanism for engaging the MILF on implementation issues, projecting continuity and renewed political commitment to implementing the CAB.
Describing the arrangement, Sarmiento said it would provide “seamless alignment” between peace policy and implementation.  His MILF counterpart, Mohagher Iqbal, offered an equally telling response: “He is a Cabinet Member: he can commit.” Civil society peace advocates also welcomed the appointment as an important step in restoring momentum to the implementation of the CAB, while emphasizing that its significance would largely depend on whether it translated into concrete progress on the CAB’s remaining commitments. These responses demonstrate the central reality of the Bangsamoro peace process: implementation of the CAB depends not only on institutions but also on confidence that those representing each party possess both the political authority and the political will to honor the commitments they made across the negotiating table.
Beyond issues like voter turnout and the absence of election-related violence, the success of the Bangsamoro’s first parliamentary elections should be judged by whether they leave behind sufficient trust for the Philippine government and the MILF to complete what remains unfinished under the CAB.

articles.title: Thailand Cracks Down on USDT Transactions in Fight Against China-linked Criminal Networks
articles.full_text:
Bangkok has been evolving toward measures that target the financial infrastructure used by region-spanning criminal networks.
On July 12, Bank of Thailand (BOT) Governor Vitai Ratanakorn announced that the BOT would begin auditing high-volume Tether (USDT) transactions. In doing so, he observed that nearly 40 percent of USDT sellers on local platforms were foreign nationals.
This decision to scrutinize transactions in USDT, a popular stablecoin, is a part of Thailand’s broader efforts to combat the financial infrastructure that enables the transnational criminal networks operating across Southeast Asia, many of which are linked to Chinese nationals or Mandarin-speaking actors. It suggests that Thai authorities are increasingly intent on disrupting the payment systems that make said criminal ecosystems possible.
In its crackdown on transnational crime, Thailand’s approach has for some time been evolving toward infrastructure-level enforcement. In the first few months of 2026, Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission filed criminal complaints against offshore digital asset operators serving Thai users without a license, while simultaneously also seeking to block unauthorized platforms from the Thai market.
These actions highlight how Thai authorities are increasingly using licensing requirements, exchange oversight, and transaction monitoring to address illicit finance before funds leave the regulated financial systems, increasing consumer protections as a whole.
These measures also coincide with recent broader enforcement efforts against gray capital, illicit remittances, and multi-channel money-laundering networks that increasingly rely on both traditional financial institutions and digital assets to move funds across borders.
The announcement of audits around USDT is part of a broader response to recent cases involving Chinese-linked actors accused of using digital assets to launder proceeds from criminal activities, including online scams, illegal gambling, and more.
These sorts of investigations have taken place repeatedly over the last year.
For example, on July 14, Thailand’s Cyber Crime Investigation Bureau announced the arrest of three suspects tied to a Chinese scam syndicate accused of laundering stolen cash into digital assets. Several weeks earlier, Thai authorities issued an arrest warrant for Chinese businessman Wang Yicheng, who has been accused of laundering money from scam operations around the world via digital asset-based financial networks based in both Thailand and China.
Last month, Thai police also arrested a Chinese national in Bangkok tied to FINTOCH, a large-scale cryptocurrency investment fraud that purported to be a high-yield crypto investment platform that promised investors “guaranteed daily returns.”
In addition to highlighting Thailand’s increasing targeting of the financial infrastructure supporting organized crime perpetuated in the cyber world, these actions also align with the trend of increased USDT usage by Chinese-linked criminal networks around the world over previously-preferred and more volatile digital currencies like Bitcoin.
In contrast, USDT’s price stability, liquidity, and rapid settlement capabilities make it well-suited for moving value across borders. Simultaneously, USDT’s current status as Asia’s, and the world’s, most popular stablecoin presents regulators with the challenging task of distinguishing illicit transactions from ordinary commercial activity.
The emphasis on cross-border capital flows suggests that Thai authorities increasingly see enforcement pertaining to digital assets as a regional security issue rather than simply a domestic law enforcement challenge. This is particularly true given the prevalence of scam compounds and quasi-legal/illicit activities in areas in neighboring Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos, all of which rely on digital assets to move ill-gotten proceeds across borders. As a result, Thailand’s financial system is now an important point of scrutiny in disrupting these wider criminal ecosystems
Thailand’s policy response also reflects the broader transformation of organized cybercrime throughout Southeast Asia. In early 2025, The Economist published a series of articles describing the epidemic of crypto-enabled “pig butchering” scams based in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos, which that rely heavily on cryptocurrency to collect victim payments, move proceeds across borders, and launder profits. Although many of these operations are located outside Thailand, their proximity and cross-border financial activity have made them a growing concern for Thai authorities.
In the backdrop of this increased regulatory oversight is Thailand’s complex relationship with China. Despite the substantial political and economic relationships between China and Thailand, Thai policymakers remain increasingly wary of China’s expanding influence.
Thailand’s increased scrutiny of financial crime linked to Chinese-origin actors should not be viewed solely through the lens of bilateral relations with Beijing.
In fact, China itself has advocated for the dismantling of these criminal networks, particularly due to Chinese citizens being direct and indirect victims of these crimes, and has put pressure on Thailand to do so. As both a regional financial hub and a close economic partner of China, Thailand’s expanding oversight of digital assets reflects the increasingly delicate balance of protecting its financial system from these aforementioned transnational criminal networks, while still maintaining support for broader regional efforts to combat cross-border financial crime.
Thailand’s scrutiny of USDT suggests that the next phase of anti-money-laundering enforcement in Asia will focus on tracing how money moves through digital assets, even if this stops short of banning them outright. The success of the Thai government in this endeavor could potentially become a model for how regulators disrupt scam-linked capital flows, with an emphasis on Chinese-linked criminal networks and their growing operations throughout Southeast Asia.
However, Thailand must do so without shutting down legitimate activity tied to digital assets, which are becoming an increasingly important tool for its traditionally financially underserved and unserved populations seeking access to cross-border payments, remittances, and other financial services.

articles.title: EU Announces New Sanctions Targeting Southeast Asia-Based Online Scam Networks
articles.full_text:
Cambodia’s Prince Holding Group and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army, a Myanmar-based rebel group, were among the targeted groups.
The European Council chamber inside the Europa building in Brussels, Belgium.
The European Union yesterday announced a fresh tranche of sanctions aimed at the operators of Southeast Asia-based online scamming operations, who they said are responsible for “serious human rights violations.”
In a statement, the European Council stated that it was imposing “restrictive measures” against seven persons and three entities in Cambodia and Myanmar, accusing them of “human trafficking, torture, and other cruel, inhuman and degrading treatments,” as well as billions of dollars in fraud.
The sanctions, which involve asset freezes and travel bans for the designated individuals and entities, are the latest response to the scamming industry that has entrenched itself across mainland Southeast Asia since the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in loosely regulated parts of Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar. Coordinated predominantly by Chinese organized crime syndicates, these industrial-scale scam operations run romance-investment and crypto scams on victims who target victims across the globe.
In addition to victimizing those on the receiving end of the scams, these rely on a large indentured workforce – mostly ordinary people who have been “trafficked or lured under false pretenses [and] held against their will,” the European Council said. Inside scam centers, victims have reported being confined in cell-like rooms, as well as subjected to beatings, mistreatment, and torture.
The new sanctions (the full Council decision is here) target the Cambodia-based Prince Holding Group and its chairman Chen Zhi. According to the EU, Prince has built scam centers in Cambodia and Myanmar under a number of front companies that “perpetrate cryptocurrency investment scams and other fraudulent schemes.” Prince Group was previously the subject of sweeping sanctions by the United States and United Kingdom, which were announced in October 2024. Shortly afterward, Chen was extradited to China, where he now faces the death penalty on a range of charges.
Another target was the Jin Bei Group, another Cambodia-based entity that has developed casinos and scam centers in the port city of Sihanoukville, and its chairman, Zhu Zhongbiao.
The other major target of the EU action was the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), an armed group that controls territory in Myanmar’s Karen State, around the border city of Myawaddy, which has grown into a pulsing hub of scam activity over the past five years.
The sanctions targeted four individuals in the DKBA’s ruling hierarchy, including Chief of Staff Saw San Sung and Major General Saw Kyaw Hla, the chairman of the DKBA’s Central Economic Committee, and Col. Saw Eh Le Htoo, the operator of the Deeko Park scam center compound.
The DKBA, which is loosely aligned with the Myanmar military, is “responsible for facilitating large-scale scam centers, by allowing these illegal compounds to operate under its protection and enabling criminal networks to function within areas under its control.” It also cited reports that the DKBA’s soldiers had participated in violence against victims trapped inside compounds on its territory.
The European Union “has consistently expressed grave concern about the proliferation of scam centers in Southeast Asia” and “underlined the need to dismantle those criminal networks, protect victims and ensure accountability for those responsible,” the Council said.
The EU has previously announced sanctions against three individuals and one entity associated with the Karen Border Guard Force (BGF), another military-aligned rebel group that controls a swath of territory along the Thai border in Karen State.

articles.title: US Aircraft Carrier USS George Washington Arrives in Vietnam on Friendship Visit
articles.full_text:
The port call, the fourth by a U.S. carrier group since 2018, is a sign that relations between Washington and Hanoi remain healthy, despite ongoing trade tensions.
The U.S. aircraft carrier USS George Washington pulls into Danang, Vietnam for a scheduled port visit, July 30, 2026.
The U.S. Navy aircraft carrier USS George Washington arrived in Danang yesterday ​for a five-day visit, a sign that relations between U.S. and Vietnam remain on track despite uncertainties in the trade relationship.
The nuclear-powered carrier and its two escorts, the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls and the guided-missile destroyer USS Shoup, pulled into the port in central Vietnam yesterday, the U.S. Pacific Fleet said in a statement.
The ship and its commanders were greeted by Vietnam’s Naval Region 3 Command, and representatives from the ministries of National Defense and Foreign Affairs, as well as senior U.S. officials from the embassy in Hanoi.
This is the fourth visit by a U.S. aircraft carrier to Vietnam since the historic visit of the USS Carl Vinson to Danang in March 2018, the first since the normalization of diplomatic relations in 1995. The USS Theodore Roosevelt then visited in March 2020, to mark the 25th anniversary of the normalization of diplomatic relations between Hanoi and Washington, followed by the USS Ronald Reagan in 2023. The Tripoli Amphibious Ready Group and 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit also paid a visit to Danang, along with the USS Robert Smalls, in December of last year.
In the statement, U.S. Ambassador Jennifer Wicks was “yet another testament” to the healthy state of U.S.-Vietnam defense cooperation and closer people-to-people ties under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership that the two nations signed in 2023.
“As we mark 250 years of American independence, we are proud to celebrate this milestone alongside our friends in Vietnam,” she said.
The USS George Washington’s port call has brought more than 5,000 sailors to Danang, where they will take part in various engagements with local leaders and the wider community.
“While our ship represents the high-end capabilities of the U.S. Navy, our visit here to Vietnam supports a U.S.-Vietnam relationship that continues to grow stronger across an increasingly broad range of subjects, reflecting our shared interest in a free and open Indo-Pacific,” Capt. Nicholas DeLeo, commanding officer of the USS George Washington, said in the statement. In its own statement, Vietnam’s Ministry of Defense ​said that the visit “contributes to maintaining and developing Vietnam-U.S. relations.”
The arrival of the George Washington reflects the two nations’ steady strategic convergence over the past two decades, driven by an overlapping, though by no means identical, concern about China’s growing power.
It also suggests that relations between Hanoi and Washington remain stable and productive, despite some turbidity in the trade relationship. Last week, the Trump administration announced a new 12.5 percent tariff on Vietnam after the conclusion of an investigation that found 60 nations had breached U.S. laws against the use of forced labor. The tariff came into effect after the expiry of a previous blanket 10 percent tariff.
The new “forced labor” tariffs are a transparent attempt by President Donald Trump to rescue his protectionist trade policy after the U.S. Supreme Court in February struck down the sweeping global tariffs that his administration imposed on allies and adversaries alike last year.
The second Trump administration has subjected Vietnam to close scrutiny on this front, given its lopsided trade surplus with the U.S., which totaled $178.2 billion in 2025, according to the U.S. Trade Representative’s office.
The continued growth of the surplus has hamstrung ongoing trade talks between the two sides, and prompted accusations in Washington that Vietnam has been used as a transshipment for Chinese goods seeking to avoid U.S. tariffs.
While Vietnam’s Foreign Ministry said that the investigation’s conclusions did not accurately reflect Vietnam’s forced labor mitigation efforts, the government last month passed a new law tightening restrictions against the import and export of goods produced with forced labor.
Vietnamese authorities also recently took the unusual step of allowing U.S. customs officials to conduct “spot checks” on Chinese-owned factories in northern Vietnam, Bloomberg reported this week. The inspectors “examined documents, raw material sources, and production processes in a bid to determine how much value was added before exporting to the U.S.,” it stated, although they did not uncover any “significant evidence of Chinese goods illicitly transiting through the country.”
The Vietnamese government is also seeking to address the long-standing U.S. concerns about intellectual property violations. After a tip-off from the U.S. government, authorities in Ho Chi Minh City recently raided a factory suspected of producing nearly 50,000 pairs of fake Nike shoes.

The arrival of the George Washington reflects the two nations’ steady strategic convergence over the past two decades, driven by an overlapping, though by no means identical, concern about China’s growing power.
It also suggests that relations between Hanoi and Washington remain stable and productive, despite some turbidity in the trade relationship. Last week, the Trump administration announced a new 12.5 percent tariff on Vietnam after the conclusion of an investigation that found 60 nations had breached U.S. laws against the use of forced labor. The tariff came into effect after the expiry of a previous blanket 10 percent tariff.
The new “forced labor” tariffs are a transparent attempt by President Donald Trump to rescue his protectionist trade policy after the U.S. Supreme Court in February struck down the sweeping global tariffs that his administration imposed on allies and adversaries alike last year.
The second Trump administration has subjected Vietnam to close scrutiny on this front, given its lopsided trade surplus with the U.S., which totaled $178.2 billion in 2025, according to the U.S. Trade Representative’s office.
articles.summary: The port call, the fourth by a U.S. carrier group since 2018, is a sign that relations between Washington and Hanoi remain healthy, despite ongoing trade tensions.

articles.title: What the Reopening of Nathu La Means for China-India Relations
articles.full_text:
Some practical cooperation is being restored between the two neighbors, despite the serious differences that remain.
The China-India border post at the Nathu La pass as viewed in 2011.
The last six years have been a testing time for China-India relations. The boundary crisis in Eastern Ladakh in 2020, along with the loss of lives in the Galwan Valley in June 2020, brought the bilateral relationship to its lowest levels in decades. Trade through Nathu La, a mountain pass through the Himalayas linking India’s Sikkim state with Tibet, also stopped in 2020. 
The meeting between Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar with China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Manila on July 22 focused on peace on the border and practical trade cooperation. A few days later, it was announced that the Nathu La pass would be reopened from August 1. This sequence of events is part of the cautious diplomacy that is now taking shape where serious differences will remain but some practical cooperation is slowly being restored.
For centuries, the route through the Chumbi Valley carried Indian textiles up into Tibet and Tibetan wool down into India via the Nathu La pass. Merchants and pilgrims walked in both directions, connecting the Bengal plains with Lhasa. The 1962 Sino-Indian war shut down that passage, and it remained closed for more than four decades. When it was reopened in 2006, it was the result of patient diplomacy rather than overwhelming commercial demand. Trade continued on a modest, seasonal basis until it was suspended in 2020, when bilateral relations were entering their most difficult phase in years. 
The opening of the Nathu La pass from August 1 is one of the dividends of the slow, cautious, and calibrated stabilization of China-India relations, which was set in motion by the meetings between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping in Kazan in 2024 and Tianjin in 2025. Direct flights resumed in October 2025, and the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra resumed in 2025 and continued this year also, while official mechanisms, academic contacts, and think-tank exchanges have also resumed. 
India’s position through this period has remained constant, and it is not just a bargaining posture. As Jaishankar put it in his July 6 meeting with Wang, “Peace and tranquility in the border areas is obviously the prerequisite for normal ties.” Therefore, the relationship can only move forward when it is built on “mutual respect, mutual interest, and mutual sensitivity.”
Border trade through Nathu La pass in the Himalayas will never resemble trade through ports or industrial corridors, because the volumes are small, the season is short, and logistics are determined by altitude and weather. But for people living on the frontier, the pass is important, since a predictable trading season gives transport operators and logistics providers work to do, and gives small businesses access to commercial activity that is difficult to sustain in remote mountain districts otherwise. 
Although the trade is seasonal and limited to designated goods, it will be transformative for the regional economy in border districts. Regular commerce helps to alleviate isolation, and gives local communities a direct stake in a stable China-India border. Trade does not generate trust overnight, but it can make cooperation appear more easy. 
The most obvious objection to the reopening of border trade at Nathu La is a matter of scale. The volume of bilateral trade between China and India is already nearing $151 billion in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while India’s deficit has reached around $112 billion. Trade at Nathu La will not bridge the gap, nor will it solve India’s concerns about market access and predictable supply chains, much less the boundary question. Therefore those issues will require sustained attention through established diplomatic and military channels. 
The biggest challenge for the reopening of the Nathu La pass is implementation of the agreement. Both sides should perhaps consider planning predictable annual calendars, transparent customs requirements, effective communication networks and adequate storage facilities. Operational issues will also require a speedy redress mechanism. Traders and local communities need to be consulted, as they are the ones who know the practical problems of the Nathu La route much better than anyone in either capital. Moreover, commercial activity at such high altitude must also take into account the fragility of the Himalayan environment. 
India and China are big neighbors whose decisions will have important consequences for the larger Asian order. Although differences will persist, including on high-stakes issues, the task of diplomacy is to engage, even as it seeks to identify areas where cooperation is possible and useful.
The traders who will cross Nathu La on August 1 will not solve the boundary question, but the reopening shows what can be accomplished when political understandings are translated into meticulous administration. Geography has often divided India and China; however, diplomacy, pursued with patience and care, might succeed in joining them again.

articles.title: North Korea Needs China and Russia – But Doesn’t Want Its People Admiring Them
articles.full_text:
Pyongyang’s strict ideological controls apply to perceptions of its allies as well as to “hostile states” like the United States.
Citizens of North Korea waving at President of Russia Vladimir Putin’s motorcade as it passes by them in Pyongyang during Putin’s state visit to North Korea, June 19, 2024. Only state-sanctioned displays of enthusiasm for Russia are permitted.
For decades, North Korean authorities have taught ordinary citizens not to harbor illusions about South Korea, the United States, and Japan, on the grounds that admiring the culture and lifestyles of “hostile states” could erode faith in the system. But recent developments inside the country suggest the authorities’ vigilance extends well beyond these so-called hostile states. Even China and Russia – partners with whom North Korea is deepening strategic cooperation – are no exception.
North Korea needs Chinese goods and capital, and is expanding military and economic cooperation with Russia. Yet it does not permit ordinary citizens to envy China’s standard of living or Russia’s technological prowess. The state may draw closer to both countries; however, its people are not allowed to hold any “illusions” about them. This contradiction reveals less about North Korea’s foreign policy than about the underlying logic that keeps its system intact.
Even a Friendly Nation May Not Be Seen However One Wishes
According to Daily NK’s reporting, the Organization and Guidance Department of North Korea’s Central Committee instructed border-area party organizations and workers’ groups in June to tighten discipline and ideological control, emphasizing that people “must not harbor illusions about Chinese-style socialism.” The move has been widely interpreted as a preemptive effort to stop North Koreans from taking interest in China’s market economy and living standards – and comparing them to conditions at home – as cross-border trade and personal exchanges with China expand.
China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and its closest socialist ally – which may be exactly what makes it such a dangerous point of comparison. People might ask: If we are both socialist countries, why can individuals in China run businesses and earn money? Why are China’s cities and villages better off than ours? Why does the state accept Chinese goods and technology while demanding that ordinary people practice total self-reliance?
A similar pattern is visible with Russia. When a new destroyer capsized during launch at the Chongjin shipyard in May 2025, some officials in the munitions sector reportedly proposed importing a large Russian crane as the most realistic way to salvage the situation. Instead, they were dismissed from their posts, and Kim Jong Un reportedly rebuked them, warning against “harboring illusions about foreign countries.” North Korea’s relationship with Russia has effectively reached the level of a military alliance – yet treating Russian technology as superior to North Korea’s own has become a political liability.
The information controls surrounding North Korea’s troop deployment to Russia fit the same pattern. Family members of deployed soldiers interviewed by Daily NK said they had not been told in advance that their sons were headed to a war zone – only that they were leaving for “study-abroad training” or “training to represent the fatherland.” Word of the deployment reached families late, not through any official notice but through letters, rumor, and word-of-mouth. Before officially acknowledging the deployment, the authorities branded the rumors as false and moved to suppress them.
AsiaPress likewise reported that, even while Pyongyang refused to officially confirm the deployment, information about casualties among North Korean troops in Russia reached the country and unsettled parents. That information is believed to have spread through South Korean broadcasts, Chinese mobile phones in border areas, and word of mouth. Facts the authorities tried to conceal reached ordinary people through multiple informal information networks.
North Korean authorities present cooperation with Russia as a diplomatic achievement of Kim Jong Un’s. But specifics – the scale of the deployment, casualty figures, how the soldiers are treated, what Russia gives North Korea in return – remain matters ordinary people are not supposed to know, let alone ask about. What Pyongyang wants is not a population devoid of pro-Russia sentiment, but one that views Russia only in the terms the authorities permit.
What North Korea Fears Is Not Information but Comparison
North Korea holds up self-reliance and self-determination as basic principles of state governance. In its view, North Korea’s problems must be solved the North Korean way, and there is no alternative to the path laid out by the party and the leader.
Within this framework, admiration for foreign countries can never remain a matter of personal taste. The moment North Koreans compare wages, consumption levels, healthcare, education, or freedom of movement and communication abroad with conditions in their country, they risk reaching conclusions the authorities never sanctioned. What threatens the system is not so much the fact that life may be better elsewhere, but the fact that a society can be run differently from North Korea’s own model.
A Korea Institute for National Unification study published last year found that as marketization and the spread of information technology converge in North Korea, outside information is flowing in quietly but deeply, and reshaping people’s perceptions and desires. Markets are not simply places to trade goods; they function as spaces where all kinds of information circulates and new lifestyles and cultural habits take root. To rein in this organic change, North Korean authorities have stepped up controls on what they label “non-socialist” and “anti-socialist” behavior.
The spread of smartphones poses a similar double-edged challenge for the authorities. 38 North reported that in 2026, smartphones are becoming increasingly embedded in North Koreans’ daily lives, with the spread of electronic wallets and mobile payments. Smartphones give the state an efficient means of managing the economy and its people – but they are also tools that let people exchange information and keep their own records.
According to AsiaPress reporting, authorities have checked the stored data on phones left at repair shops and caught people who had watched Chinese films. Authorities have inspected phones simply because their owners had taken photographs on the street. Sources say even photographing homeless people, market price tags, or the scene of an accident can bring on a crackdown. Phone ownership is permitted, but using a phone to document and share reality is not.
The Korea Institute for National Unification’s White Paper on North Korean Human Rights 2025 likewise noted that, since 2021, North Korea has toughened penalties for foreign culture and expression through special laws such as the Reactionary Ideology and Culture Rejection Law and the Pyongyang Cultural Language Protection Law – some of which prescribe the death penalty. North Korea treats access to information and freedom of expression as crimes that threaten the security of the system.
This tightening of control does not indicate that the ideological foundations of North Korea’s system are solid – if anything, the opposite is more likely true. Repeated lectures, censorship, punishment, and mutual surveillance are necessary precisely because the authorities judge that mere exposure to life abroad could unsettle people ideologically. That’s why isolation, repression, and fear have deepened in North Korea over the past decade, according to the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights.
What North Korea’s government fears most is not simply outside information. It is the process that follows – a North Korean citizen believing that information, comparing it with their own life, discussing it with others, and concluding that North Korea’s problems might have different solutions. What the authorities are trying to monopolize is not information alone, but people’s right to interpret it.
What North Koreans Need May Not Simply Be More Information
This reality poses an important challenge for efforts aimed at changing North Koreans’ consciousness.
First, simply increasing the volume of outside information is not enough. What is needed is concrete information people can directly compare with their own daily lives: how Chinese workers are paid and how they spend their wages, how Russian workers stay in touch with their families, what responsibilities hospitals and schools bear in other countries, and what steps governments take when disaster or food shortages strike.
China and Russia can serve as especially valuable points of comparison. Because Pyongyang officially presents both as friendly nations, it is harder for the authorities to dismiss information about them as “hostile propaganda” the way they can with material about South Korea or the United States. Of course, China and Russia should not be portrayed as ideal societies – both countries have their own problems with corruption, inequality, and human rights. But the simple fact that citizens of North Korea’s own allies enjoy more choice than North Koreans do in work, income, movement, and communication can raise important questions.
The content of that information should not stay at the level of abstract explanations of freedom and democracy. It should start from concrete problems of daily life: why workers are not paid their wages in full, why North Koreans must cover the operating costs of hospitals and schools, and why the state negotiates freely with foreign countries while blocking people from calling family members abroad.
It is also worth guarding against the impulse to inject a predetermined conclusion into North Koreans’ minds. Rather than repeating the verdict that “the North Korean system is wrong,” it is more important to give people the facts and questions they need to judge reality for themselves. Those who convey information should not hand down conclusions on North Koreans’ behalf, but should provide the standards people can use to compare and judge for themselves.
At the same time, the media outlets and sources that report from inside North Korea deserve more attention. Without the reporting done by outlets such as Radio Free Asia and AsiaPress, it would be far harder to grasp the specifics of Pyongyang’s double standard toward China and Russia, and how North Koreans are responding to it. Reporting from inside North Korea is as much about carrying North Koreans’ voices and realities out to the wider world as it is about bringing outside information in. Protecting sources must remain the top priority, alongside building long-term systems for documentation and cross-verification.
North Korea accepts Chinese and Russian technology and resources, even as it tries to stop people from measuring North Korea against the realities of those two countries. The conclusion this contradiction points to is clear: what North Korean authorities fear most is not outside information itself, but the possibility that North Koreans will use it to compare and judge their own reality.
That makes the international community’s own task clear as well. The goal is not to hand North Koreans an answer we have already settled on, but to give them the facts – and a safe channel – through which they can question, compare, and reach conclusions on their own. If what North Korea fears most is comparison, then what we should prepare most seriously for is making that comparison possible.
For decades, North Korean authorities have taught ordinary citizens not to harbor illusions about South Korea, the United States, and Japan, on the grounds that admiring the culture and lifestyles of “hostile states” could erode faith in the system. But recent developments inside the country suggest the authorities’ vigilance extends well beyond these so-called hostile states. Even China and Russia – partners with whom North Korea is deepening strategic cooperation – are no exception.

articles.title: Why Did China Test a Submarine-launched Ballistic Missile?
articles.full_text:
July 6 was the first time that China has launched a submarine-launched ballistic missile into international waters.
On July 6 China tested a submarine-launched intercontinental ballistic missile into the South China Sea. A PLA statement after the test claimed that “the missile test was a routine part of China’s annual military training program, and relevant countries had been notified in advance.” 
In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics Podcast, hosts Ankit Panda and Katie Putz take stock of the test and the reactions across the Pacific. July 6 was the first time that China has launched a submarine-launched ballistic missile into international waters, and only its the second launch of a ballistic missile into international waters since 1980. Also unusual: China provided notice to Australia, Japan, the United States, and others, through in some cases only half an hour.

articles.title: Europe’s China Strategy Is Ready for a Refresh
articles.full_text:
EU leaders have an opportunity to stop treating repression as a side issue and instead make human rights more central to their engagement with China.
At the European Council on June 19, EU leaders gave the European Commission a clear mandate to develop additional trade defense instruments to protect its markets against subsidized imports. At the Franco-German Ministerial Council on July 16-17, for the first time after years of division on the issue, France and Germany jointly identified China  as “challenging our economy” and called for the establishment of an EU roadmap to protect European industries against Chinese competition.

At the Franco-German Ministerial Council on July 16-17, for the first time after years of division on the issue, France and Germany jointly identified China  as “challenging our economy” and called for the establishment of an EU roadmap to protect European industries against Chinese competition. 
At the European Council on June 19, EU leaders gave the European Commission a clear mandate to develop additional trade defense instruments to protect its markets against subsidized imports. At the Franco-German Ministerial Council on July 16-17, for the first time after years of division on the issue, France and Germany jointly identified China  as “challenging our economy” and called for the establishment of an EU roadmap to protect European industries against Chinese competition. 
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker summarized it all: “The EU needs to have a strategic reorientation.”    Europe’s responses to Beijing’s long-term industrial planning has deepened Europe’s dependence on its trade with China with a focus on matters like subsidies or overcapacity, market distortions, and unfair competition. However, any shift in Europe’s approach to China needs to elevate human rights.    The truth is that China’s economy and industry are intertwined with the Chinese government’s human rights abuses. State-imposed forced labor, forced labor transfers of Uyghur workers, the prohibition on independent unions, forced land seizures or coerced relocations have all featured in industries key to China’s relationship with Europe, from electric battery production, to solar and renewable energy supply chains, to technology.    Meanwhile, vague criminal offenses, mass surveillance, and pervasive repression allow Chinese authorities not only to silence critics, but also to reshape communities and entire industries with little resistance.    European governments have, in effect, turned a blind eye to these human rights violations as some of Europe’s most important industries sought access to Chinese markets and Chinese suppliers. These include strategic sectors such as automotive or critical raw materials needed for electronic products and batteries.    Furthermore, Beijing has now made it harder for European institutions and companies to scrutinize and respond to its human rights abuses. Coercive practices that primarily targeted Chinese lawyers, activists, and political opponents are now increasingly targeting foreign companies and their staff through extraterritorial measures.    In addition to existing laws restricting cross-border transfer of data and technology by defining vague offenses, Beijing has passed new decrees to prevent foreign companies from pressing for transparency in their supply chains and from identifying risks of forced labor or other abuses linked to Chinese government policies. This includes trying to block foreign companies that try to stop sourcing from Chinese suppliers linked to human rights abuses. The Chinese Communist Party’s coercive logic is no longer contained within China’s borders: it is being externalized to the operating environment of European firms.    The European Commission has developed a set of “Trade Defense” tools, such as safeguard measures, anti-dumping, or anti-subsidy duties. But the Commission proposals do not address the deeper, structural, and intertwined nature of the Chinese Communist Party’s authoritarian model with its economic policies. As long as the EU isolates human rights from trade, procurement, industrial policy, and security, it will keep underestimating the nature of the challenge.    Instead, European countries should further integrate human rights issues in their economic and foreign policy with China.    In particular, they should strengthen the EU regulation banning products made with forced labor by allowing for region-wide bans on products made through state-imposed forced labor in Xinjiang or through labor transfers. By robustly enforcing human rights due diligence legislation, including the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, EU governments can both push Chinese companies in Europe to respect their obligations and ensure that European companies press their suppliers in China, and elsewhere, to meet robust human rights standards.    The EU should further invoke labor protections embedded in International Labor Organization conventions and trade agreements China has signed. It should also press Beijing to allow independent unions and account for rights-abusing-subsidies when qualifying their impact in specific sectors.    The bloc should also raise related human rights concerns at each high-level talk on trade and security. And it should sanction Chinese entities implicated in abuses or surveillance and exclude them from EU and member states procurement processes.    The Chinese government’s human rights abuses should not be isolated from Europe’s interests. EU leaders have an opportunity to stop treating repression as a side issue and instead make human rights more central to their engagement with China. They should work jointly to harmonize their policies, so that together, they can resist the Chinese government’s retaliation and foster a more human-rights aligned trade ecosystem. 
Hélène de Rengervé is a senior advocate on corporate accountability at Human Rights Watch.
Maya Wang is deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
articles.summary: EU leaders have an opportunity to stop treating repression as a side issue and instead make human rights more central to their engagement with China.

articles.title: Resilience at the Heart of Australia-Singapore Ties
articles.full_text:
At the 15th Singapore-Australia Joint Ministerial Committee this week, the two sides emphasized resilience across sectors, from defense to trade.
This week the 15th Singapore-Australia Joint Ministerial Committee (SAJMC) was held in Adelaide, South Australia. The SAJMC is held every two years and brings together senior ministers from both governments to coordinate cooperation across the full spectrum of the relationship, rather than focusing on a single policy area. This year, it was attended by both countries’ respective ministers for foreign affairs, defense, and trade. 
The centerpiece of the discussions was the signing of a new Protocol on Economic Resilience and Essential Supplies. This was a signal that both countries are viewing their national security now not solely in terms of traditional defense, but in terms of securing essential goods that are required to maintain services and standards of living. 
The new protocol is designed to ensure that cooperation on essential goods continues to flow between the two countries during periods of global disruption. There is a particular focus on energy security, given that over half of Australia’s petroleum imports are refined in Singapore, while around a third of Singapore’s LNG usage is supplied by Australia. The protocol establishes the Australia-Singapore Economic Resilience Dialogue, which is a dedicated mechanism for the two countries to discuss their shared challenges and build practical cooperation. 
The creation of such a mechanism reflects the current era, where major disruptions are now expected rather than seen as isolated events. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how quickly governments could restrict the export of medical equipment and other critical goods. The current war in the Middle East has highlighted how reliant the world is on energy flows, and how a more globally destabilized environment may make such wars more frequent. 
Importantly, the two countries are not advocating for economic disengagement from the broader global trading system. Both repeatedly emphasize their support for open, rules-based commerce, with the World Trade Organization remaining the central mechanism for trade disputes. What Australia and Singapore are seeking to create is a backstop where trusted partners can cooperate if other systems are impacted or fail. 
This focus on economic resilience also extends into the signed Industrial Base Resiliency Arrangement (IBRA). This arrangement is designed to improve resilience in defense supply chains in order to strengthen the two countries’ defense industrial cooperation. This will allow “both countries to engage in cross-sustainment of common defense platforms, examine priority delivery requests for defense orders, streamline equipment transfers, foster defense industry partnerships, and facilitate information exchanges to mitigate supply chain risk.”
This further entrenches the close defense relationship between the two countries. This has developed not only through a similar outlook on the world, but through practical necessity. Singapore has an unmatched defense footprint in Australia because it has almost no space to train a modern military, while Australia has an abundance of land. Singapore maintains permanent training presences at two Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) bases – Oakey Army Aviation Center in Queensland, where its Air Force helicopters fleet trains, and RAAF Base Pearce near Perth, where it conducts fixed-wing fighter training. 
Defense cooperation in conjunction with supply chain resilience underpins how Australia and Singapore see the most pressing regional concern in the South China Sea – a waterway both countries are dependent on. The joint communiqué firmly expressed “the importance of the right of unimpeded transit passage of vessels and aircraft in straits used for international navigation in accordance with international law as reflected in UNCLOS.” It also raised “serious concern over behavior that increased the risk of miscalculation and unilateral actions that could threaten peace, security, and stability in the South China Sea.”
Australia and Singapore already had a close relationship. The existence of the SAJMC is illustrative of this. The meeting’s purpose now is to look for ways to enhance the relationship through the lens of a more unstable world. Creating more formal processes gives both countries more predictability in a crisis, and sets up more issue-specific consultation mechanisms that can respond quickly and effectively to shocks. 
This sits within a broader outlook for countries like Australia and Singapore, which have some strong capabilities but are far from being powers that can exert their will upon the Indo-Pacific region. Instead they are looking to shape the environment where they can, and develop the structures that allow them to navigate the world with greater confidence through coordinated responses. 
This week the 15th Singapore-Australia Joint Ministerial Committee (SAJMC) was held in Adelaide, South Australia. The SAJMC is held every two years and brings together senior ministers from both governments to coordinate cooperation across the full spectrum of the relationship, rather than focusing on a single policy area. This year, it was attended by both countries’ respective ministers for foreign affairs, defense, and trade. 
The centerpiece of the discussions was the signing of a new Protocol on Economic Resilience and Essential Supplies. This was a signal that both countries are viewing their national security now not solely in terms of traditional defense, but in terms of securing essential goods that are required to maintain services and standards of living. 
The new protocol is designed to ensure that cooperation on essential goods continues to flow between the two countries during periods of global disruption. There is a particular focus on energy security, given that over half of Australia’s petroleum imports are refined in Singapore, while around a third of Singapore’s LNG usage is supplied by Australia. The protocol establishes the Australia-Singapore Economic Resilience Dialogue, which is a dedicated mechanism for the two countries to discuss their shared challenges and build practical cooperation. 
The creation of such a mechanism reflects the current era, where major disruptions are now expected rather than seen as isolated events. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how quickly governments could restrict the export of medical equipment and other critical goods. The current war in the Middle East has highlighted how reliant the world is on energy flows, and how a more globally destabilized environment may make such wars more frequent. 
Importantly, the two countries are not advocating for economic disengagement from the broader global trading system. Both repeatedly emphasize their support for open, rules-based commerce, with the World Trade Organization remaining the central mechanism for trade disputes. This will allow “both countries to engage in cross-sustainment of common defense platforms, examine priority delivery requests for defense orders, streamline equipment transfers, foster defense industry partnerships, and facilitate information exchanges to mitigate supply chain risk.”
This further entrenches the close defense relationship between the two countries. This has developed not only through a similar outlook on the world, but through practical necessity. Singapore has an unmatched defense footprint in Australia because it has almost no space to train a modern military, while Australia has an abundance of land. Defense cooperation in conjunction with supply chain resilience underpins how Australia and Singapore see the most pressing regional concern in the South China Sea – a waterway both countries are dependent on. The joint communiqué firmly expressed “the importance of the right of unimpeded transit passage of vessels and aircraft in straits used for international navigation in accordance with international law as reflected in UNCLOS.” It also raised “serious concern over behavior that increased the risk of miscalculation and unilateral actions that could threaten peace, security, and stability in the South China Sea.”
Australia and Singapore already had a close relationship. The existence of the SAJMC is illustrative of this. The meeting’s purpose now is to look for ways to enhance the relationship through the lens of a more unstable world. articles.title: Can Southeast Asia Overcome the Middle-Income Trap?
articles.full_text:
Southeast Asian nations won’t overcome the middle-income trap unless predatory elites stop undermining education and R&D.
High rates of economic growth in Southeast Asia in recent decades have led to rising income levels within the region. Yet few Southeast Asian countries have been able to move beyond middle-income status to achieve high-income status in the World Bank’s country income classifications, reflecting the fact that economic growth rates in the region have slowed since the late 1990s. 
Today, only Singapore and Brunei are classified as high-income countries. Other countries in the region are either lower-middle income countries (Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Timor-Leste, the Philippines, Vietnam) or upper-middle income countries (Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia). 
Moreover, some middle-income Southeast Asian countries have remained stuck at their current levels for many years. The Philippines, for instance, has been a lower-middle income country since the late 1970s while Malaysia has been an upper-middle income country since 1992. Timor-Leste, Thailand, Lao PDR and Vietnam have all been at their current levels since the late 2000s.
This situation has led some economic analysts to question whether the region is succumbing to the so-called “middle-income trap.” According to the World Bank — which coined the term — the middle-income trap is a systematic growth slowdown due to an inability “to take on the new economic structures needed to sustain high-income levels.” These structures include sound infrastructure, strong institutions, low levels of corruption, and policy settings that encourage technology transfer. But, perhaps most importantly, they include strong education and Research and Development (R&D) ecosystems capable of driving innovation. Such ecosystems are currently weak in most Southeast Asian countries.
Unfortunately, the region will find it difficult to address this education and R&D deficit because the political preconditions for change are absent. Specifically, the region lacks what political scientists Richard Doner and Ben Ross Scheidner have referred to as powerful “upgrading coalitions” — that is, coalitions of political and social groups that have an interest in improved educational and R&D systems and can drive change in these systems.
In recent decades, Southeast Asian countries have greatly improved access to education, including for the poor. However, this has not been accompanied by significant improvement in educational quality in much of the region.
One sign of this is the region’s poor performance in international standardized assessments of school-level student achievement such as PISA, PIRLS and TIMSS. Wealthy Singapore and Brunei have fared well in these assessments, as has Vietnam. But other participating middle-income countries — the Philippines, Indonesia, Cambodia, Thailand, and Malaysia — have generally clustered towards the bottom of these league tables. 
The lack of education quality is also reflected in global university rankings. Singaporean universities — particularly the National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University — rate among the top universities in the world. But only eight Southeast Asian universities appear in the top 500 in the most recent Times Higher Education World University rankings. One of these is Universiti Brunei Darussalam while two are from Singapore and five are from Malaysia. 
Finally, the region’s R&D systems lack dynamism. According to the Global Innovation Index (GII), the region as-a-whole performs poorly in all seven areas covered: institutions, human capital and research, infrastructure, market sophistication, business sophistication, creative outputs, and knowledge and technology outputs. 
Unfortunately, there is no easy fix to these weaknesses, in no small part due to the politics involved.
The ascendance of predatory political, bureaucratic and corporate elites stymies reform. Their primary interests lie in the status quo — the extraction of rents from natural resources sectors, the exploitation of low-wage and low-skilled labor, and control over or privileged access to state facilities, budgets, appointments, contracts, and concessions. 
Some of these elites have been involved in education sectors in their respective countries as owners of private education institutions, senior education administrators, and/or contractors to education departments and institutions. Yet, they have largely sought to use education systems to accumulate resources, distribute patronage, mobilize political support, and exercise political control rather than produce skilled workers, encourage critical and inquiring minds, and stimulate innovation. 
They accordingly have little interest in providing the financial, human resource, incentive structure and administrative prerequisites for a high-quality education system and stronger learning outcomes. Nor have they had much interest in strong R&D ecosystems due to their focus on rent-seeking rather than innovation. 
Technocratic elements in government and the international financial institutions have contested this orientation seeking a stronger focus on basic skills acquisition in the name of market efficiency. Progressive elements have done likewise, in the name of human rights and social justice. But both elements have lacked the leverage required to drive through their preferred changes. 
At the same time, progressive elements have often opposed the market-oriented education policy reforms promoted by technocratic elements, claiming these reforms promote the commercialization and privatisation of education and worsen education inequality. These two sets of elements have yet to evolve into a powerful “upgrading coalition.”
Indonesia provides an illustration. The Asian economic crisis and fall of the New Order in 1997-1998 precipitated the introduction of a series of technocratic education policy reforms, many promoted by the World Bank. These included corporatization of public educational institutions, a new teacher certification scheme, a competency-based curriculum, and a high stakes national exam. But continued predatory dominance combined with democratisation meant that predatory and progressive elements were able to contest these reforms, leading in many cases to their partial or full defeat.
Vietnam has been an exception, notwithstanding the dominance of a predatory/authoritarian elite based in the Communist Party of Vietnam. This is because technocratic elements have had greater sway over education policy and its implementation than in Southeast Asia’s other middle-income countries; and the absence of democracy has limited the scope for progressive elements to push back against technocratic reform. 
The Communist Party has made spending on education a priority, outlaying almost 5.7 percent of Gross Domestic Product on education in 2017, much higher than Indonesia (3.6 percent in 2015) and the Philippines (2.6 percent in 2012). Vietnam has prioritised investment in pre-school, primary and basic literacy education, promoted equity in access, and attracted and supported qualified teachers. 
Efforts to improve education and R&D ecosystems in the region will need to go beyond increased public education and R&D funding, additional administrative capacity, improved teaching training, and the removal of disincentives to change — the measures emphasized in technocratic analyses — and promote a fundamental reconfiguration of power relations between these elements. 
They will need to consider ways of ensuring technocratic and/or progressive elements in these countries become stronger than predatory political bureaucratic and corporate elites in their influence over education and R&D policy and its implementation while forging a common platform for change.
Such change, while difficult, is fundamental to addressing the middle-income trap.
